reviewed_source_excerpts: Use natural units $c=\hbar=1$ on the four-dimensional affine Minkowski space $M=\mathbb R^{1,3}$ with metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, as in the selected HEFT spacetime convention. Use the trivial spin structure, spinor bundle $S=M\times\mathbb C^4$, gamma matrices satisfying $\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}I$, chirality operator $\gamma_5=i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3=-i\gamma_0\gamma_1\gamma_2\gamma_3$, and eigensubbundles $S_\pm=\ker(\gamma_5\mp I)$. Here $\gamma_0=-\gamma^0$, $\gamma_j=\gamma^j$ for spatial $j$, and $\bar\psi=\psi^\dagger i\gamma^0$; choose $(i\gamma^0)^\dagger=i\gamma^0$ and $(\gamma^j)^\dagger=\gamma^j$. This matches the shared anomaly-matching data and Bilal's mostly-plus positive-chirality convention in Eq. (2.20), which fixes the sign of his anomaly formula. Take the trivial bundle for the fixed global symmetry group $H=SU(3)\times U(1)_V$, set the $SU(3)$ background connection to zero, and keep only the nondynamical $U(1)_V$ connection $B\in\Omega_c^1(M,\mathbb R)$ with curvature $G=dB$. Here $U(1)_V=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ and its charge-$q$ representation is $\rho_q(z)=z^q$ on $\mathbb C$. The background $B$ is not integrated over as a quantum gauge redundancy.

Fix the complex exterior algebra $\Lambda=\bigwedge_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\xi_a,\bar\xi_a:a\in\mathbb N\}$, with algebraic finite sums, and let $\Lambda_{\mathrm{odd}}$ be its odd-degree subspace. Conjugation is the antilinear involution exchanging $\xi_a$ and $\bar\xi_a$ and reversing product order. Let $\psi_+\in C_c^\infty(M,S_+\otimes\mathbb C_{(\mathbf1,+1)})\otimes_{\mathbb C}\Lambda_{\mathrm{odd}}$ and $\psi_-\in C_c^\infty(M,S_-\otimes\mathbb C_{(\mathbf1,0)})\otimes_{\mathbb C}\Lambda_{\mathrm{odd}}$ be Weyl fields: finite sums of smooth compactly supported sections with Grassmann-odd coefficients in the indicated representations. Odd coefficients anticommute; the Dirac adjoint uses this conjugation and the spinor adjoint. This implements the shared anomaly-matching data's fermionic statistics for both the charged field and its neutral mass partner; the determinant and measure below remain formal perturbative inputs, not integrals over a fixed finite set of generators. Use $D_q=d+iqB$ on charge-$q$ fields and the fixed Lorentz-scalar chiral Dirac pairing $\bar\psi_+\psi_-$. Let $\Phi=v e^{i\theta}$ be a nonvanishing order-parameter field in $(\mathbf1,+1)$ with fixed modulus $v>0$ and smooth real phase $\theta\in C_c^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. A dimensionless nonzero Yukawa parameter $y$ gives the mass term $-y\Phi\bar\psi_+\psi_-+\mathrm{h.c.}$, where h.c. denotes Hermitian conjugation, and heavy mass $M_H=|y|v>0$. The fermion fields have mass dimension $3/2$, $v$ and $M_H$ have mass dimension one, $B_\mu$ has mass dimension one, $G_{\mu\nu}$ has mass dimension two, and $\theta$ is dimensionless.

For $\alpha\in C_c^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, use $B\mapsto B+d\alpha$, $\psi_+\mapsto e^{-i\alpha}\psi_+$, $\psi_-\mapsto\psi_-$, and $\Phi\mapsto e^{-i\alpha}\Phi$, hence $\theta\mapsto\theta-\alpha$. These transformations leave the Yukawa term invariant. In the anti-Hermitian product-group convention, the selected singlet has connection $iB$ and covariant derivative $d+iB$; in Bilal's Hermitian convention write $\mathscr A=-B$ and $\epsilon=-\alpha$, so $d-i\mathscr A=d+iB$ and the transformations agree. Let $\Gamma_H[B,\theta]$ denote the formal one-loop effective-action contribution of this Yukawa-massive pair, whose fermion mass is $M_H=|y|v>0$. For determining its local consistent-anomaly coefficient, separately use the Pauli–Villars-regulated one-loop triangle with one gauge-current insertion and two $U(1)_V$ background-connection insertions for a massless positive-chirality Weyl field in $(\mathbf1,+1)$. In this triangle calculation only, the physical loop has $M_0=0$ and weight $\eta_0=1$, while the three regulator loops have weights $\eta_1=\eta_3=-1$ and $\eta_2=1$, a positive scale $M_{\mathrm{PV}}$, and masses $M_1=M_3=M_{\mathrm{PV}}$, $M_2=\sqrt2M_{\mathrm{PV}}$, with $M_{\mathrm{PV}}\to\infty$ after subtraction. The $M_0=0$ physical loop belongs only to this massless triangle calculation; it is not the physical loop of $\Gamma_H$, whose mass remains $M_H>0$. Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{tri},0}(\alpha,B)$ denote the local consistent-anomaly variation computed from this massless triangle. It fixes the massless chiral representation's coefficient and is not the variation of the massive pair or a definition of its full determinant. Define the consistent anomaly as an infinitesimal effective-action variation, rather than as a covariant-current divergence. Add no non-invariant local counterterm to $\Gamma_H$; gauge-invariant local counterterms may be added. For an undetermined real coefficient $c$, the candidate Wess–Zumino functional is $\Gamma_c[B,\theta]=c\int_M\theta G\wedge G$; the theorem on this page fixes $c$.

Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff $\chi$ that equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\alpha$, with $\alpha\geq0$. Let $\lambda>0$ have mass dimension two and set $B=\lambda\chi(x)(x^0dx^1+x^2dx^3)$, normalizing $\alpha$ so that $\lambda^2\int_M\alpha\,d^4x=1$. For the charge-one positive-chirality field, neutral mass partner, and $M_H>0$ of the stated formal model, this evaluates the exact local identity from the preceding theorem. It makes no assertion about a finite-momentum vertex or the Fourier support of the chosen compactly supported backgrounds. The consistent heavy-sector and Wess–Zumino variations are equal, nonzero, and each equal $+1/(12\pi^2)$.
**Given:** The theorem's charge, transformation, and consistent-anomaly convention, together with the smooth compactly supported cutoff and normalized nonnegative test parameter.

reviewed_source_excerpts:
Let $H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b_{T,c}(X;\mathbb Q)}(\mathbb Q_X,\omega_X^T[-j])$, where $\omega_X^T$ is the normalized equivariant dualizing object whose restriction is the ordinary dualizing object $\omega_X$, without a quotient-stack dimension shift. Equivalently, this is the stable value in degree $j$ of $H^{\mathrm{BM}}_{j+2rm}(X_m;\mathbb Q)$, where $U_m=(\mathbb C^{m+1}\setminus\{0\})^r$ has the free right scalar $T$-action, $X_m=(U_m\times X)/T$ uses $(e,x)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)$, and the supplied bounded-Hom comparison is taken in its stable range. Put $H_*^{\mathrm{BM},T}(X;\mathbb Q)=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}H_j^{\mathrm{BM},T}(X;\mathbb Q)$. Pullback from $B_K$ and cap product make this total group an $R_T$-module: a homogeneous $a\in R_T^q$ sends $H_j$ to $H_{j-q}$, so coefficients have homological degree $-q$. For an $R_T$-module $M$, $S_T^{-1}M$ consists of fractions $m/s$ with $m\in M$, $s\in S_T$, and $m/s=m'/s'$ exactly when some $t\in S_T$ satisfies $t(s'm-sm')=0$; addition and scalar multiplication are the induced fraction operations. Localize the total graded module and define
$$
\mathcal H_j^T(X):=\left(S_T^{-1}H_*^{\mathrm{BM},T}(X;\mathbb Q)\right)_j.
$$
For homogeneous $\beta\in H_k^{\mathrm{BM},T}(X;\mathbb Q)$ and $s\in S_T$ of cohomological degree $q$, the fraction $\beta/s$ has homological degree $k+q$. The notation $S_T^{-1}H_j^{\mathrm{BM},T}(X;\mathbb Q)$ will mean $\mathcal H_j^T(X)$, never localization of the individual group $H_j$. Likewise localized equivariant cohomology means localization of $\bigoplus_q H_T^q(X;\mathbb Q)$ with $\deg(\alpha/s)=\deg\alpha-\deg s$. Cap product extends by $(\alpha/s)\cap(\beta/t)=(\alpha\cap\beta)/(st)$. At a point, $H_j^{\mathrm{BM},T}(\mathrm{pt};\mathbb Q)=H^{-j}(B_K;\mathbb Q)$, so $\mathcal H_j^T(\mathrm{pt})=(S_T^{-1}R_T)^{-j}$. Proper equivariant maps induce degree-preserving pushforwards, invariant open inclusions induce Borel–Moore restrictions, and a smooth pure $d$-dimensional complex variety has its complex-oriented fundamental class $[X]_T$ in degree $2d$. For $r=0$, $R_T=\mathbb Q$ and $S_T=\{1\}$.

3.1 The operations in the Definition are the proper pushforward, open restriction, and support maps of [F2]; the cap action is the action of Borel cohomology through $E_K\times_KX\to B_K$. For smooth pure complex dimension $d$, the normalized dualizing object restricts to $\mathbb Q_X[2d]$, so the complex orientation gives $[X]_T$ degree $2d$. These constructions respect the stable comparison of [F1]. For homogeneous $a\in R_T^q$, cap product lowers homological degree by $q$. In the fraction relation, all denominators are homogeneous; if two homogeneous fractions have different degrees, multiply to a common denominator and compare homogeneous components. Equality then forces each fraction to be zero. Splitting a numerator into its finitely many homogeneous components therefore gives the stated direct grading of the localization, with $\deg(\beta/s)=\deg\beta+\deg s$. The cap fraction formula is well-defined because cap product is balanced over the even-degree coefficient ring: a multiplier annihilating either numerator relation also annihilates the corresponding cap relation. Proper pushforward and open restriction commute with coefficient cap products, so they extend to the localized total modules and preserve their homogeneous pieces. [F1, F2, step 1.2] ∎

reviewed_source_excerpts: 1.1 The set $D(f)$ is $T$-invariant because $f(t\cdot x)=\chi(t)f(x)$. On its Borel construction, define $s([e,x])=[e,f(x)]$ in the associated character line. This is well-defined: replacing $(e,x)$ by $(e\cdot t,t^{-1}\cdot x)$ replaces $f(x)$ by $f(t^{-1}\cdot x)=\chi(t)^{-1}f(x)$, exactly the right equivalence $(e,z)\cdot t=(e\cdot t,\chi(t)^{-1}z)$. Since $f$ never vanishes on $D(f)$, $s$ is a nowhere-zero section and trivializes that line bundle. The same formula trivializes its restriction to every $T$-invariant open $V\subseteq D(f)$. To ensure the preceding definition applies to $V$, write $D(f)=\operatorname{Spec}A_f$. Its coordinate ring is graded by the character lattice $\mathbb Z^r$, and the ideal $I(Z)$ of the invariant closed complement $Z=D(f)\setminus V$ is homogeneous. For each $x\in V$, choose $g\in I(Z)$ with $g(x)\neq0$; a homogeneous component $g_\lambda\in I(Z)$ also satisfies $g_\lambda(x)\neq0$. The principal open $D(g_\lambda)$ is invariant, affine, contains $x$, and lies in $V$. Since $D(f)$ is noetherian, its open subset $V$ is quasi-compact, so finitely many such principal opens cover $V$. Thus $V$ has a finite invariant affine cover. [A1, F1, construct]

3.1 Since $\chi$ is nontrivial, $u_\chi\in S_T$ is invertible after localization. For any class $\beta$, its localized image satisfies $\beta/1=(u_\chi\cap\beta)/u_\chi=0$ by step 2.1. Every homogeneous fraction is $\beta/s=(\beta/1)/s$, so the localized total modules, and hence all their degree pieces, vanish on both $D(f)$ and $V$. If the opposite character convention is used, the class is $-u_\chi$, which is also in $S_T$ up to the unit $-1$ and has the same annihilation consequence. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $T=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act algebraically on a separated finite-type complex variety $X$ that admits a finite cover by $T$-invariant affine open subvarieties. Let $F=X^T$ be the fixed-point subscheme, $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ its closed inclusion, and let $S_T$ be the character multiplicative set in the localized equivariant Borel–Moore definition. Write $S_T^{-1}H_j^{\mathrm{BM},T}(Y;\mathbb Q)=\mathcal H_j^T(Y)$ for the degree-$j$ piece of the localization of the total graded Borel–Moore module, for $Y=F,X$. Then in every homological degree $j$, proper pushforward induces an isomorphism
$$
i_*:S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q).
$$
No compactness of $X$, normality hypothesis, or compact-orbit-type nilpotence hypothesis is required.

3.1 For a finite invariant open cover of $X\setminus F$, the augmented Čech complex with terms $j_{I!}\mathbb Q_{D_I}$, where $D_I$ is an intersection and $j_I:D_I\hookrightarrow X\setminus F$ is open, resolves the constant equivariant sheaf. At a point the indices containing it form a nonempty simplex, whose augmented chain complex is contracted by adjoining its least index. Applying derived Hom into the normalized dualizing object gives a finite Čech spectral sequence for Borel–Moore homology: open base change identifies each term with the Borel–Moore group of an intersection $D_I$. Those groups vanish after localization by [F2]. Take the direct sum over all homological degrees in each term, so that the spectral sequence consists of $R_T$-modules with homogeneous differentials. Since the Čech filtration is finite and localization of these total modules is exact by [F4], taking the homogeneous degree pieces gives that the abutment $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F;\mathbb Q)$ is zero for every $j$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Apply exact localization to the total graded closed/open sequence and then take homogeneous pieces. The resulting closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 3.1] ∎

Let $T=(\mathbb C^\times)^r$ act on a smooth separated finite-type complex variety $X$ with a finite invariant affine open cover. Let $F=X^T$ be proper, $i:F\hookrightarrow X$, $p_F:F\to\mathrm{pt}$, and $S_T$ the character multiplicative set. Every notation $S_T^{-1}H_j^{\mathrm{BM},T}(Y;\mathbb Q)$ below means $\mathcal H_j^T(Y)$, the degree-$j$ piece of the localization of the total graded module. By the finite-affine-atlas concentration isomorphism, $i_*:S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F;\mathbb Q)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)$ is invertible. Define the intrinsic localized pushforward
$$
p^{\mathrm{loc}}_*:=p_{F*}\circ(i_*)^{-1}:S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(\mathrm{pt};\mathbb Q),
$$
where $p_{F*}$ is the genuine proper Borel–Moore pushforward. For a homogeneous $\alpha\in H_T^q(X;\mathbb Q)$ and smooth complex dimension $d$, an allowed insertion is $\alpha\cap[X]_T\in H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{2d-q}(X;\mathbb Q)$; the fundamental class $[X]_T$ is the complex-oriented class, not the cohomological unit $1\in H_T^0(X;\mathbb Q)$. This construction does not define an ordinary pushforward along a nonproper map $X\to\mathrm{pt}$.

1.1 By [F2], $i_*$ is an isomorphism in each degree after localization, and on the total graded localization its inverse is a unique degree-preserving $S_T^{-1}R_T$-linear map; its restrictions give the degree-$j$ inverses. The proper inclusion $i$ and the proper map $p_F$ give the stated Borel–Moore pushforwards by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, given]

reviewed_source_excerpts: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix an integer $N\ge2$. Write $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ for the complex $N\times N$ matrices, $U^*=\overline U^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and $I_N$ for the identity matrix. Define the special unitary matrix group

with matrix multiplication and the following real embedded smooth structure. Identify $\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$ by the real and imaginary matrix entries, and let $\operatorname{Herm}_N=\{H:H^*=H\}$ have its induced real vector-space structure. Equip $U(N)=\{U:U^*U=I_N\}$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $I_N$ of the smooth map $F:\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)\to\operatorname{Herm}_N$, $F(U)=U^*U$, where $\operatorname{GL}_N(\mathbb C)=\{U:\det U\ne0\}$. Equip $S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with its embedded circle structure and $SU(N)$ with the embedded regular-level-set structure at $1$ of $\det:U(N)\to S^1$. These are the embedded structures in the stated real matrix space. Its real Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{su}(N):=\{X\in\operatorname{Mat}_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X,\ \operatorname{tr}X=0\}$ with bracket $[X,Y]=XY-YX$. The standard unitary representation is the map $\rho:SU(N)\to U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ defined by $\rho(U)v=Uv$, where $h(v,w)=\sum_{j=1}^N\overline{v_j}w_j$ and $U(\mathbb C^N,h)$ consists of the complex-linear maps preserving $h$. Conjugation is $\operatorname{Ad}_U z=UzU^{-1}$ for either $z\in SU(N)$ or $z\in\mathfrak{su}(N)$.

Let $M$ be a compact, connected, oriented, boundaryless smooth manifold of dimension $d\in\{3,4\}$ with a smooth Riemannian metric, and fix a smooth right principal $SU(N)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$, a smooth connection $A_0$, and a point $p_m\in P$ over $x_m\in M$. Use the representation $\rho$ and the invariant positive inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle=-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$. Define the adjoint vector bundle $\operatorname{ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the adjoint group bundle $\operatorname{Ad}P=P\times_{\operatorname{Ad}}SU(N)$ with associated-bundle relation $[pg,z]=[p,\operatorname{Ad}_g z]$.
